summary: Deep technical session focused on Private VPC deployment networking (PrivateLink, NAT, subnets, DNS) and runtime tradeoffs (KV cache, batching, quantization). Team discussed latency/throughput SLOs, cross-AZ egress patterns, and pilot benchmark plan.
topics: NAT vs egress through managed gateways
Runtime performance: batching, KV cache, quantization
Latency vs cost tradeoffs and pilot benchmarks
Security controls: KMS, audit logs, SOC2
transcript: 00:00:02 - Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're scheduled for 60 minutes, I'll let Samir drive the technical deep dive.
00:00:12 - Lena Ortiz: Hi, Lena from Aurelius, CTO. We manage sensitive patient workflows and evaluating Private deployments. We have Ravi and Emma on the infra and ML sides.
00:00:22 - Ravi Kumar: Ravi here, infra lead. We're mostly AWS, VPC spanning three AZs, current NAT gw for egress, and peering with our analytics account.

00:00:28 - Samir Patel: Great, thanks. I'll outline typical Redwood Private VPC patterns then dig into runtime tradeoffs - KV cache, batching, quant, and how that interacts with networking like PrivateLink and NAT.
00:01:05 - Emma Zhou: Quick ask up front - our main worry is p95 latency under load. We run real-time summarization so 200-300ms p95 is ideal, anything above impacts UX.

00:01:22 - Samir Patel: Totally get it. Let's set expectations: hosted endpoints have different egress paths; Private uses PrivateLink or VPC endpoints to keep traffic inside your network. Latency budgets are influenced by placement of model serving, batch windows, and whether KV cache hits avoid remote reads.
00:02:05 - Maya Chen: And just to note, we often pair AE + SE: I'll handle commercial follow-ups, Samir will capture the technical bits.

00:02:34 - Samir Patel: Slide one - typical Private deployment. We run a control plane outside, but compute plane sits in your VPC. You get an ENI-backed PrivateLink endpoint so control messages and metrics can traverse securely. There's also an optional NAT egress for pulling model artifacts or OS updates.
00:03:01 - Ravi Kumar: On artifact pulls - we prefer restricting internet egress. Can Redwood pull models via a dedicated S3 role or do we need open NAT?

00:03:10 - Samir Patel: You can use S3 VPC endpoints and role-based access, or we can push artifacts via a signed bundle through PrivateLink. Both patterns are supported; the latter avoids NAT entirely.
00:03:42 - Lena Ortiz: What's the overhead of PrivateLink ENIs? We have tight IP allotment in some subnets.

00:03:51 - Samir Patel: ENIs are lightweight but you do need IPs per AZ per endpoint. If IP scarcity is an issue, we recommend a dedicated subnet for Redwood runtimes with /23 or larger depending on expected workers. We can also collapse into fewer AZs for initial pilot.
00:04:28 - Emma Zhou: For runtime - KV cache, is that local to the GPU host, or a remote cache? We do a lot of conversation continuation so compressing prefix tokens matters.

00:04:39 - Samir Patel: Good question. Our KV cache is local to the serving instance's memory; it's in-process per serving worker. That means cache hits are local and zero-network. Cache sharing across hosts is possible but adds network RTT, so generally we prefer local warm caches and routing affinity for sessions that need low latency.
00:05:20 - Ravi Kumar: So session affinity requires sticky routing - is that through our load balancer or Redwood's routing plane?

00:05:29 - Samir Patel: Redwood's routing layer can request sticky routing by session ID; if you want to enforce at LB level, we support that too. For cross-AZ affinity there's a trade: keeping to same AZ avoids cross-AZ egress costs and latency, but reduces resilience if AZ drops.
00:06:02 - Maya Chen: Quick interruption - Emma you mentioned target p95 200-300ms; is that for short sequences? If you go to 1k tokens, obviously p95 will be higher.
00:06:12 - Emma Zhou: Right, our average request is 60 tokens with bursts to 512 for longer summarizations. We care most about the 60-token flow.

00:06:35 - Samir Patel: For that profile, we can optimize for low-latency by lowering batch windows (e.g., 10-20ms), enabling KV cache warm-up, and using a quantized model variant. But quantization can change quality; we'll run evals on your prompt set.
00:07:05 - Ravi Kumar: How much does quantization buy us on CPU/GPU cost vs latency?

00:07:15 - Samir Patel: On GPUs with tensor cores, int8 quantization can reduce memory bandwidth and improve throughput by 1.5x-2x depending on model. Latency per token can drop ~10-30% for inference paths that are memory-bound. But it's model and HW dependent.
00:07:46 - Emma Zhou: Any effect on deterministic outputs? We rely on stable summaries for compliance.

00:07:55 - Samir Patel: There can be small distributional shifts. That's why Redwood Optimize suggests a quantization profile and runs regressions against eval sets; we gate production rollouts on quality regressions.
00:08:30 - Lena Ortiz: Back to networking - DNS. We had issues with split-horizon DNS previously. How do you recommend configuring resolution for PrivateLink endpoints and internal metrics endpoints?

00:08:44 - Samir Patel: We recommend conditional forwarding: your internal resolver forwards the redwood domain to the VPC resolver which resolves to private IPs. Alternatively, we provide explicit PrivateLink hostnames and you can add A records in Route53 private hosted zones.
00:09:12 - Ravi Kumar: Does Redwood require outbound connections for healthchecks? We prefer inbound-only for some subnets.

00:09:22 - Samir Patel: Healthchecks can be either direction. We support agent-based outbound health telemetry through PrivateLink, or you can configure our control plane to ping an endpoint in your VPC that replies - both methods avoid internet egress.
00:10:01 - Emma Zhou: On batching - what's the default batching window and how configurable is it? We worry about jitter causing latency spikes.

00:10:12 - Samir Patel: Default continuous batching is adaptive. For low-latency needs we allow you to set hard max_batch_latency (e.g., 10-30ms) and max_batch_size. We also have predictive batching where we pre-allocate small batches for steady state requests to avoid cold latency spikes.
00:10:44 - Ravi Kumar: How do you observe per-token latency? We need tracing to tie slowdowns to network vs compute.

00:10:53 - Samir Patel: Redwood Console emits per-request spans: request entrance, routing, batch queueing, kernel execution, and response streaming. Traces can be forwarded to your X-Ray/Datadog via PrivateLink or to S3 for audits.
00:11:30 - Lena Ortiz: For compliance, we need audit logs and KMS integration for model keys. Does Redwood integrate with our KMS/HSM?

00:11:40 - Samir Patel: Yes, we support customer-managed keys with KMS, and can integrate HSM-backed key stores for private deployments. All models and encryption keys are audited; we can ship logs into your Splunk/S3 via PrivateLink.
00:12:12 - Maya Chen: Quick note - action item to share a SOC2 summary specific to Private deployments. I think we have a redwood-soc2-private.pdf link.
00:12:22 - Emma Zhou: Great. For the pilot, what does a minimal subnet layout look like?

00:12:30 - Samir Patel: Minimal: one subnet per AZ dedicated to Redwood workers, each /24 for light pilots but we recommend /22 or /21 for production scale. Control plane PrivateLink can live in a management subnet. NAT can be avoided if you use S3 endpoints and artifact push via PrivateLink.
00:13:05 - Ravi Kumar: Cross-AZ traffic - if a session is routed to an instance in another AZ, what's the latency penalty? We have 2-3 ms intra-AZ, and 6-12 ms cross-AZ typically.

00:13:17 - Samir Patel: Right, cross-AZ adds a few ms and also incurs egress costs. For strict p95 SLAs we recommend AZ affinity. For high availability we do multi-AZ fallback where we prefer local AZ but route to another on failure.
00:13:50 - Lena Ortiz: What about model versioning and rollouts in Private? We need to pin versions and gradually roll new quantized models.

00:14:00 - Samir Patel: You can pin model versions per route and do canary rollouts by traffic percentage. Our runtime supports serving multiple variants with automated fallback when a variant is overloaded.
00:14:30 - Emma Zhou: Curious about the KV cache warm-up strategy - if we route a user to a warm host, that's great, but for new sessions how long until cache is effective?

00:14:40 - Samir Patel: Warm-up depends on prefix length. For short contexts caching helps mostly for multi-turn. We offer persistent session caches that keep hot sessions resident for N minutes; for workload with repeated patterns, cache hit rate can be 60-80% after warm-up.
00:15:12 - Ravi Kumar: Benchmarking plan? We want to validate p95 and throughput for 60-token typical load and 512 token bursts.

00:15:22 - Samir Patel: We'll run a pilot with two phases: latency-focused (low batch latency, warm cache) and throughput-focused (higher batch windows, more concurrency). We'll measure p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and cost per 1M tokens. Samir to run initial internal baseline and then coordinate remote runs in your VPC.
00:16:04 - Maya Chen: I'll coordinate pricing scenarios once scope is set. Any regulatory items - data residency or retention?
00:16:12 - Lena Ortiz: We need logs retained 7 years for certain audit trails and need to ensure PHI never leaves our VPC unencrypted in transit or at rest.

00:16:25 - Samir Patel: We can enforce TLS+mutual auth over PrivateLink, and keys are customer managed. Logs to S3 stay in your account. For long retention we can keep a second copy to archival S3 with lifecycle rules.
00:17:00 - Emma Zhou: One more runtime point - kernel selection and sequence-length optimizations. Do you compile kernels per model or use a generic engine?

00:17:13 - Samir Patel: Our compilation picks optimal kernels based on architecture and sequence length histograms. For your workload we'll collect sample sequences, and we can generate a tuned kernel set that reduces per-token latency.
00:17:45 - Ravi Kumar: If we want on-prem instead of VPC, are the networking constraints similar?

00:17:54 - Samir Patel: On-prem introduces more manual networking: you host control endpoints, and we provide an appliance that negotiates with your LAN. PrivateLink isn't a thing on-prem, but we support direct peering/VPNs and explicit hostnames for service discovery.
00:18:30 - Lena Ortiz: Last block - failure modes. If an AZ goes down, do requests fail open to hosted or queue?

00:18:40 - Samir Patel: We offer configurable fallback policies: failover to another AZ instance (possible cross-AZ latency), degrade to smaller models to maintain latency, or route to hosted endpoints as last resort - all configurable per-route.
00:19:05 - Emma Zhou: Ok that's useful. For the pilot, we'll try both AZ-affinity and a fallback policy to measure UX.

00:19:18 - Maya Chen: Recap and next steps: Samir shares runbook/diagram, Ravi sends VPC details, Emma provides prompt set, Samir runs internal baseline and coordinates pilot schedule. We'll aim to start pilot week of 2027-01-10. Any final Qs?
00:19:38 - Lena Ortiz: Not from me. Thanks, that was thorough.
00:19:42 - Ravi Kumar: Thanks - I'll put the subnet map in the doc today.
00:19:45 - Maya Chen: Great. I'll follow up with the pricing deck and SOC2 doc.
00:19:50 - Samir Patel: Thanks everyone, I'll send the architecture diagram and a short checklist for NAT/PrivateLink decisions.
00:20:00 - [meeting ends into side chatter and hold music - transcript ends shortly after]
